title: Z-Cache: Accelerating Diffusion Transformers via Self-Reflection

paper.title: Z-Cache : Accelerating Diffusion Transformers via Self-Reflection
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion transformers have become the most powerful models for visual generation, but still suffer from massive computation costs. To solve this problem, feature caching has been proposed to cache the features of diffusion models in the previous computation steps and then reuse them in the following caching steps, which brings significant acceleration but also degradation in generation quality. To address this problem, this paper proposes Z-cache as a feature caching method that can maintain high-quality generation through self-reflection. Concretely, we observe that the error from feature caching tends to be sharply reduced after each full computation. Based on this observation, Z-Cache is designed to first predict the features in the future caching steps and then perform a full computation. After that, Z-Cache returns to the caching steps and re-predicts them based on the previous and the current computation steps, which brings correction in features. Experiments demonstrate that with Z-Cache , diffusion transformers achieve comparable generation quality to the original model but with faster inference speed, for instance, 6.22 × \times acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation. Our code is released on GitHub . Figure 2 : Visualization of the per-layer L1 error from feature caching. It is observed that there exists a periodic decline in L1 error, which is caused by the full-computation step in feature caching. The proposed Z-Cache utilizes this phenomenon and derives fewer cumulative errors.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) have become a dominant paradigm for high-quality visual generation, but their iterative denoising process remains computationally expensive, especially for high-resolution image and video synthesis. This cost limits practical deployment and motivates a broad set of acceleration methods. Among them, feature caching ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025c ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025d ) is particularly attractive because it is training-free: instead of running the full denoising network at every timestep, it reuses or predicts intermediate hidden states across nearby timesteps. The key assumption behind feature caching is temporal redundancy. Hidden states at adjacent denoising steps are often similar, allowing expensive transformer blocks to be skipped with minor quality loss. However, this assumption becomes fragile under aggressive acceleration. As the cache interval grows, single-anchor reuse or forecasting accumulates hidden-state errors, which can lead to semantic drift, local artifacts, and degraded prompt fidelity. This creates a central trade-off: larger cache windows improve efficiency but increasingly deviate from the true denoising trajectory. We start from a simple empirical observation. As shown in Figure 2 , cache-induced feature error tends to grow within each cache window, but drops sharply when a scheduled full-computation step is performed. This suggests that full-computation anchors partially pull the accelerated trajectory back toward the original denoising path. Rather than only using a full step as the starting point for the next cache window, we ask whether the newly obtained future anchor can also be used to correct the provisional states inside the previous active window. Based on this observation, we propose Z-Cache , a training-free and predictor-agnostic reflection framework for diffusion feature caching. For each active cache window, Z-Cache first uses a base cache predictor to forecast intermediate hidden states from a past full-computation anchor and runs the corresponding provisional denoising transitions. After reaching the next scheduled full-computation anchor, Z-Cache revisits the same window, estimates each intermediate hidden state with both the past and future anchors, and re-samples the window trajectory before committing the reflected window-end latent. Therefore, Z-Cache is not a post-hoc smoothing operation over already generated samples. Instead, it is an in-loop trajectory correction mechanism that changes the subsequent denoising path. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Z-Cache in text-to-image, text-to-video, and image editing tasks, as well as its compatibility with other feature caching methods and other diffusion acceleration methods such as step distillation and quantization. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify a cache-induced error pattern in diffusion feature caching: hidden-state errors tend to accumulate within a cache window but are sharply reduced after scheduled full-computation anchors, which motivates using future anchors to correct the previous active cache window. • We propose Z-Cache , a training-free cache-then-check framework that performs dual-anchor reflection and active-window re-sampling. Unlike post-hoc smoothing, Z-Cache revises the latent trajectory inside the denoising loop and continues sampling from the reflected window-end state. • We establish Z-Cache as a plug-and-play and composable acceleration module. It can be attached to compatible feature-cache predictors, generalizes beyond free-form generation to image editing and video synthesis, and remains compatible with orthogonal acceleration techniques such as few-step distillation and low-bit quantization.

sections.heading: Feature caching
sections.text: Feature caching accelerates diffusion sampling by reusing or predicting intermediate activations. It spans U-Net models ( Li et al., 2023a ; Ma et al., 2024 ) , DiT representation reuse ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024c ) , adaptive timestep caching ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , token-wise or dual feature caching ( Zou et al., 2024a ; Zou et al., 2024b ) , and predictors such as TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025c ) , SpeCa ( Liu et al., 2025d ) , and MagCache ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . SenCache ( Haghighi and Alahi, 2026 ) adapts reuse using sensitivity estimates, D2Cache ( Liu et al., 2026 ) improves temporal prediction with second-order deltas, and ResCa ( Fang et al., 2026 ) updates tokens using proxy-guided residuals.

sections.heading: Positioning of Z-Cache
sections.text: Z-Cache performs cache-then-check correction: after observing the next scheduled full-computation anchor on the provisional trajectory, it combines past- and future-anchor predictions, replays the closed provisional window, and continues from the reflected endpoint. This complements compatible cache policies and predictors while preserving the full-computation schedule; composition requires compatible cached representations and state updates. Appendix A.1 provides a detailed taxonomy and comparisons.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: Figure 3 : Pipeline of Z-Cache. The figure uses the reverse-diffusion notation t , t − 1 , … t,t-1,\ldots for visualization, while the text uses a sampling-order index that increases along denoising. Traditional feature caching forecasts an active window from a past full-computation anchor and directly moves to the next window. In contrast, Z-Cache treats the window as provisional: after obtaining the next scheduled full-computation anchor, it revisits the same window, constructs dual-anchor hidden estimates, re-samples the window trajectory, and commits the reflected window-end latent. Z-Cache therefore performs in-loop trajectory correction without adding extra full-computation steps.

sections.heading: 3.3 Z-Cache
sections.text: Z-Cache is a training-free reflection wrapper for feature caching. It does not prescribe a specific cache predictor; instead, it can be applied on top of a base predictor 𝒞 \mathcal{C} such as TaylorSeer, SpeCa, or MagCache. The key idea is to treat the states inside the current cache window as provisional until the next scheduled full-computation anchor is available. After obtaining that future anchor, Z-Cache revisits the active window, constructs dual-anchor hidden estimates, re-samples the window trajectory, and then continues denoising from the reflected state.

sections.heading: Active cache window.
sections.text: Consider one active cache window [ a , b ] [a,b] in sampling-order indices. Full hidden states are computed at the endpoint anchors a a and b b , while the intermediate indices a < i < b a<i<b are cached. Let 𝒜 a \mathcal{A}_{a} denote the anchor set available before entering this window, which includes the past anchor a a . The window proceeds in three stages.

This full computation is part of the original cache schedule, so Z-Cache does not add extra scheduled full-computation steps.

This distinguishes Z-Cache from post-hoc hidden-state smoothing: the reflected hidden estimates affect later outputs because they are used to re-run the latent transitions inside the active window.

Specifically, we run FLUX-Kontext-dev on the Gedit-bench benchmark and compare Z-Cache with TaylorSeer, as summarized in Table 4(c) . At the same acceleration ratio, Z-Cache achieves higher PSNR and SSIM while substantially reducing LPIPS. These improvements indicate that Z-Cache better preserves the source image’s structure and perceptual details, which are crucial for maintaining subject identity and keeping non-edited background regions consistent. We further compare Z-Cache with non-caching acceleration methods in Table 4(b) . The results show that Z-Cache is complementary to quantization: adding Z-Cache on top of 8-bit quantization (8bit Z-Cache ) increases the speedup from 2.10 × \times (8bit only) to 3.12 × \times , while also improving PSNR and reducing LPIPS. Under the same 3.12 × \times acceleration budget, 8bit Z-Cache consistently outperforms 8bit TaylorSeer across all four metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and ImageReward), indicating that the reflection step provides non-trivial gains even when the backbone is already compressed. In contrast, a distilled model such as Flux-mini achieves a comparable speedup (3.80 × \times ) but with substantially worse fidelity and preference scores, suggesting that cache-based acceleration remains competitive in the high-speed regime. Overall, these results support the view that Z-Cache is not a replacement for quantization/pruning, but a plug-in that can be layered on top of them. We additionally evaluate Z-Cache on SDXL , a U-Net-based diffusion model, and directly compare it with TaylorSeer under matched step budgets (i.e., the same cache-step setting). As summarized in Table 4(d) , Z-Cache consistently improves PSNR and SSIM, reduces LPIPS, and achieves higher ImageReward than TaylorSeer across both acceleration ratios, while using the same number of cache steps. These results indicate that the proposed cache-then-check mechanism generalizes beyond DiT-style backbones and naturally transfers to U-Net architectures. Additional trajectory controls, fusion and replay ablations, and recent-predictor compositions are reported in Appendix A.3 .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper introduces Z-Cache , a novel caching framework that redefines the efficiency-quality trade-off for diffusion transformers. Central to its innovation is a self-reflective mechanism, which periodically refines intermediate features through "future-aware" feature integration—enabling substantial acceleration without sacrificing output fidelity. By integrating this mechanism, Z-Cache achieves exceptional acceleration (up to 6.22× faster inference on FLUX-dev.1) while preserving high output quality. Beyond static image generation, Z-Cache demonstrates remarkable adaptability to video tasks, attaining a state-of-the-art 6.20× acceleration rate for videos, all while maintaining high output quality.

sections.heading: Diffusion models and diffusion transformers.
sections.text: Diffusion models [ Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 , Ho et al., 2020 ] generate data through iterative denoising and have become a dominant framework for visual generation. Early systems were largely based on U-Net architectures [ Ronneberger et al., 2015 ] , while recent large-scale models increasingly adopt diffusion transformers (DiTs) [ Peebles and Xie, 2023 ] . This architectural shift has enabled strong image and video generation performance across modern systems [ Chen et al., 2024b , Chen et al., 2024a , Zheng et al., 2024 , Yang et al., 2025 ] . However, the iterative sampling process remains computationally expensive, motivating two broad acceleration directions: reducing the number of sampling timesteps and reducing the per-step cost of the denoising network.

sections.heading: Sampling timestep reduction.
sections.text: Timestep reduction methods aim to preserve generation quality with fewer denoising iterations. DDIM [ Song et al., 2021 ] introduces deterministic sampling for faster inference, while DPM-Solver and its variants [ Lu et al., 2022b , Lu et al., 2022a , Zheng et al., 2023 ] use high-order ODE solvers to reduce the number of function evaluations. Rectified Flow [ Liu et al., 2023 ] learns straighter paths between noise and data, and distillation-based approaches compress multi-step generation into fewer steps [ Salimans and Ho, 2022 , Meng et al., 2022 ] . Consistency Models [ Song et al., 2023 ] further enable one-step or few-step generation by directly mapping noisy inputs to clean outputs. These methods reduce sampling length and are orthogonal to our goal of improving feature caching within a given sampling schedule.

sections.heading: Denoising network acceleration.
sections.text: Another line of work accelerates the denoising network at each timestep. Compression-based methods include pruning [ Fang et al., 2023 , Zhu et al., 2024 ] , quantization [ Li et al., 2023b , Shang et al., 2023 , Kim et al., 2025 ] , distillation [ Li et al., 2023c ] , and token reduction or token merging [ Bolya and Hoffman, 2023 , Kim et al., 2024 , Zhang et al., 2024 , Zhang et al., 2025 , Cheng et al., 2025 , Saghatchian et al., 2025 ] , alongside dynamic-resolution approaches [ Zheng et al., 2026a , Yan et al., 2026 , Zheng et al., 2026b , Qin et al., 2026 ] . These approaches reduce computation by simplifying model weights, activations, or token sequences. Although effective, they often require tuning, calibration, or careful engineering to maintain the quality–efficiency balance. Z-Cache is complementary to these methods because it is training-free and modifies the inference-time feature-caching trajectory rather than the model parameters.

sections.heading: Feature caching-based acceleration.
sections.text: Feature caching exploits temporal redundancy across diffusion timesteps to accelerate inference [ Liu et al., 2025b , Liu et al., 2025a ] . Early caching methods for U-Net diffusion models include Faster Diffusion [ Li et al., 2023a ] and DeepCache [ Ma et al., 2024 ] . Recent methods extend this idea to transformer-based diffusion models. FORA [ Selvaraju et al., 2024 ] and Δ \Delta -DiT [ Chen et al., 2024c ] reuse attention or representation states across nearby steps. TeaCache [ Liu et al., 2024 ] uses timestep-adaptive caching, while ToCa and DuCa [ Zou et al., 2024a , Zou et al., 2024b ] cache token-wise or dual feature representations. Other methods improve efficiency through error-aware caching, adaptive caching-pruning combinations, or spatially varying sampling strategies [ Qiu et al., 2025 , Sun et al., 2025 , Liu et al., 2025f ] .

sections.heading: Forecasting and predictor-oriented caching.
sections.text: More recent feature-caching methods improve the base cache predictor itself [ Zheng et al., 2025a , Cai et al., 2026 , Shen et al., 2026b , Zou et al., 2026 , Shen et al., 2026a ] . TaylorSeer [ Liu et al., 2025c ] predicts intermediate features using polynomial extrapolation from neighboring cached activations, which establishes the cache-then-forecast paradigm. SpeCa [ Liu et al., 2025d ] introduces speculative feature caching, and MagCache [ Ma et al., 2025 ] exploits magnitude-aware caching for efficient generation. These works primarily focus on improving feature prediction or cache scheduling.

sections.heading: Sensitivity-aware, second-order, and spatial residual caching.
sections.text: Recent methods address different sources of caching error. SenCache [ Haghighi and Alahi, 2026 ] estimates how denoising outputs respond to changes in the latent input and timestep, and uses these sensitivities to decide whether cached outputs can be reused for each sample. Its sensitivity estimates are obtained using a small calibration set. D2Cache [ Liu et al., 2026 ] augments a cached first-order residual with a second-order residual difference and scales this correction using error estimates derived from timestep embeddings. ResCa [ Fang et al., 2026 ] exploits similarity among token denoising trajectories: it computes a proxy token for each cluster and uses multi-order residuals to guide simulated updates of the remaining tokens. Its updates combine a token’s historical residuals with current residual information from the proxy. These approaches respectively emphasize sensitivity-guided cache decisions, temporal residual prediction, and spatially shared denoising information.

sections.heading: Relation to Z-Cache.
sections.text: Z-Cache performs retrospective trajectory correction within an active cache window. Once the next scheduled full-computation anchor is observed on the provisional trajectory, Z-Cache combines past-anchor and future-anchor predictions, replays the window, and commits the reflected endpoint before continuing denoising. This differs from SenCache’s reuse decisions, D2Cache’s temporal extrapolation, and ResCa’s current-step proxy-guided token updates. Z-Cache can therefore complement compatible cache policies and predictors while preserving the base full-computation schedule, provided their cached representations and state updates support dual-anchor prediction and window replay.

sections.text: We conducted experiments mainly on three state-of-the-art diffusion architectures: DiT-XL/2 [ Peebles and Xie, 2023 ] , FLUX.1-dev [ Black Forest Labs, 2024 ] , and HunyuanVideo [ Kong et al., 2024 ] . sections.text: We evaluate text-guided image generation on FLUX.1-dev with DrawBench. Each method generates 200 images at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 resolution using the default sampling configuration. To make the efficiency comparison explicit, we report end-to-end H100 latency, peak CUDA memory, and FLOPs under the same implementation. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are computed against the corresponding full 50-step FLUX.1-dev outputs under the same prompts and seeds, while ImageReward is computed on generated image–prompt pairs.

sections.heading: A.5 Impact Statement
sections.text: This work improves the efficiency of diffusion-model inference via a training-free caching-and-reflection strategy ( Z-Cache ). By reducing the compute and latency required per generated sample, it can lower energy use and broaden access to high-quality generative models for research and practical applications. However, cheaper and faster generation may also enable misuse (e.g., large-scale misinformation, deceptive or non-consensual synthetic media, and spam) and can amplify existing concerns such as bias or copyright infringement. Z-Cache does not change the underlying model’s training data or safety properties, so responsible deployment should rely on standard safeguards such as access controls, rate limiting, moderation/filtering, and provenance mechanisms where appropriate.

Corresponding author Abstract Diffusion transformers have become the most powerful models for visual generation, but still suffer from massive computation costs. To solve this problem, feature caching has been proposed to cache the features of diffusion models in the previous computation steps and then reuse them in the following caching steps, which brings significant acceleration but also degradation in generation quality. To address this problem, this paper proposes Z-cache as a feature caching method that can maintain high-quality generation through self-reflection. Concretely, we observe that the error from feature caching tends to be sharply reduced after each full computation. Based on this observation, Z-Cache is designed to first predict the features in the future caching steps and then perform a full computation. After that, Z-Cache returns to the caching steps and re-predicts them based on the previous and the current computation steps, which brings correction in features. Experiments demonstrate that with Z-Cache , diffusion transformers achieve comparable generation quality to the original model but with faster inference speed, for instance, 6.22 × \times acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation. Figure 1 : Images sampled by 6.22 × \times accelerated FLUX.1-dev with Z-Cache . 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) have become a dominant paradigm for high-quality visual generation, but their iterative denoising process remains computationally expensive, especially for high-resolution image and video synthesis. This cost limits practical deployment and motivates a broad set of acceleration methods. Among them, feature caching ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025c ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025d ) is particularly attractive because it is training-free: instead of running the full denoising network at every timestep, it reuses or predicts intermediate hidden states across nearby timesteps. The key assumption behind feature caching is temporal redundancy. Hidden states at adjacent denoising steps are often similar, allowing expensive transformer blocks to be skipped with minor quality loss. However, this assumption becomes fragile under aggressive acceleration. As the cache interval grows, single-anchor reuse or forecasting accumulates hidden-state errors, which can lead to semantic drift, local artifacts, and degraded prompt fidelity. This creates a central trade-off: larger cache windows improve efficiency but increasingly deviate from the true denoising trajectory. We start from a simple empirical observation. As shown in Figure 2 , cache-induced feature error tends to grow within each cache window, but drops sharply when a scheduled full-computation step is performed. This suggests that full-computation anchors partially pull the accelerated trajectory back toward the original denoising path. Rather than only using a full step as the starting point for the next cache window, we ask whether the newly obtained future anchor can also be used to correct the provisional states inside the previous active window. Based on this observation, we propose Z-Cache , a training-free and predictor-agnostic reflection framework for diffusion feature caching. For each active cache window, Z-Cache first uses a base cache predictor to forecast intermediate hidden states from a past full-computation anchor and runs the corresponding provisional denoising transitions. After reaching the next scheduled full-computation anchor, Z-Cache revisits the same window, estimates each intermediate hidden state with both the past and future anchors, and re-samples the window trajectory before committing the reflected window-end latent. Therefore, Z-Cache is not a post-hoc smoothing operation over already generated samples. Instead, it is an in-loop trajectory correction mechanism that changes the subsequent denoising path. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Z-Cache in text-to-image, text-to-video, and image editing tasks, as well as its compatibility with other feature caching methods and other diffusion acceleration methods such as step distillation and quantization. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify a cache-induced error pattern in diffusion feature caching: hidden-state errors tend to accumulate within a cache window but are sharply reduced after scheduled full-computation anchors, which motivates using future anchors to correct the previous active cache window. • We propose Z-Cache , a training-free cache-then-check framework that performs dual-anchor reflection and active-window re-sampling. Unlike post-hoc smoothing, Z-Cache revises the latent trajectory inside the denoising loop and continues sampling from the reflected window-end state. • We establish Z-Cache as a plug-and-play and composable acceleration module. It can be attached to compatible feature-cache predictors, generalizes beyond free-form generation to image editing and video synthesis, and remains compatible with orthogonal acceleration techniques such as few-step distillation and low-bit quantization. 2 Related Works Feature caching Feature caching accelerates diffusion sampling by reusing or predicting intermediate activations. It spans U-Net models ( Li et al., 2023a ; Ma et al., 2024 ) , DiT representation reuse ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024c ) , adaptive timestep caching ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , token-wise or dual feature caching ( Zou et al., 2024a ; Zou et al., 2024b ) , and predictors such as TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025c ) , SpeCa ( Liu et al., 2025d ) , and MagCache ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . SenCache ( Haghighi and Alahi, 2026 ) adapts reuse using sensitivity estimates, D2Cache ( Liu et al., 2026 ) improves temporal prediction with second-order deltas, and ResCa ( Fang et al., 2026 ) updates tokens using proxy-guided residuals. Positioning of Z-Cache Z-Cache performs cache-then-check correction: after observing the next scheduled full-computation anchor on the provisional trajectory, it combines past- and future-anchor predictions, replays the closed provisional window, and continues from the reflected endpoint. This complements compatible cache policies and predictors while preserving the full-computation schedule; composition requires compatible cached representations and state updates. Additional trajectory controls, fusion and replay ablations, and recent-predictor compositions are reported in Appendix A.3 . 5 Conclusion This paper introduces Z-Cache , a novel caching framework that redefines the efficiency-quality trade-off for diffusion transformers. Central to its innovation is a self-reflective mechanism, which periodically refines intermediate features through "future-aware" feature integration—enabling substantial acceleration without sacrificing output fidelity. By integrating this mechanism, Z-Cache achieves exceptional acceleration (up to 6.22× faster inference on FLUX-dev.1) while preserving high output quality. Beyond static image generation, Z-Cache demonstrates remarkable adaptability to video tasks, attaining a state-of-the-art 6.20× acceleration rate for videos, all while maintaining high output quality.
